subtitulo: Sixty-eight Indigenous languages, four Spanish accents you will actually notice, and one word in the right place that changes a whole exchange
cena: The woman at the stall said something to the man beside her that was not Spanish, and she is now turning back to you as if nothing happened.
frasePiso: One word, in the right region, said small and without a performance. That is the entire technique, and it is enough.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Mexico officially recognises 68 Indigenous languages alongside Spanish. Nahuatl has roughly 1.7 million speakers, concentrated in central Mexico, and the Maya languages follow, with over 800,000 speakers across the Yucatán Peninsula.
fatosDatados.fonte: Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI); descrições de consenso sobre línguas do México

fatosDatados.afirmacao: In Yucatec Maya, dyos bo'otik is a widely used way of saying thank you — a Spanish-Maya hybrid form, with yuum bo'otik as the more traditional variant. In Nahuatl, tlazocamati serves as thank you.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de fontes regionais (Yucatán Today — «Say It in Maya»; Na'atik Language & Culture Institute; recursos de náhuatl da COERLL/UT Austin)

steps.pt: Spanish is not the only language in the room. Today is mostly listening, with one small production move at the end.
At a stall in Yucatán, the woman says something to the man beside her that isn't Spanish, then turns back to you.
👂 Yucatec Maya: how are you, roughly. Nothing to do — just notice it happened.
Mexico recognises sixty-eight Indigenous languages. Nahuatl has about 1.7 million speakers, the Maya languages over 800,000.
That switch wasn't secrecy. Bilingual people move between languages by who they're addressing.

steps.promptPt: Ask what language that was — curious, not startled. Speak now.
steps.pt: What language is that?

steps.es: Es maya. Aquí casi todos lo hablamos.
steps.pt: It's Maya. Almost all of us here speak it.
steps.tts: Es maya. Aquí casi todos lo hablamos.

steps.pt: Now the accents. Central runs fast and clipped, the coast sings, the Yucatán carries Maya rhythm, the north has its own pull.
👂 Central. Fast, clipped, mande as the polite catch-all.

steps.es: ¿Qué onda, qué te vas a llevar, pariente?
steps.pt: 👂 Northern. Different rhythm, different address word. Same request.
steps.tts: ¿Qué onda, qué te vas a llevar, pariente?

steps.pt: The one production move: a courtesy word. In the Yucatán, dyos bo'otik is thank you. In Nahuatl country, tlazocamati.

steps.promptPt: You're in the Yucatán and she just helped you. Thank her in Maya. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you (Yucatec Maya).
Oh, you speak Maya!
Say the honest thing back. One word is one word, and claiming more than that is how a nice moment turns awkward.

steps.promptPt: Correct the compliment, warmly. Speak now.
steps.es: Solo esa palabra, pero la quería decir bien.
steps.pinyin: SOH-loh EH-sah pah-LAH-brah, PEH-roh lah keh-REE-ah deh-SEER byen
steps.pt: Only that word — but I wanted to say it properly.
steps.tts: Solo esa palabra, pero la quería decir bien.

steps.promptPt: Ask her to teach you one more, and to correct your pronunciation. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me enseña otra? Dígame si lo digo mal.
steps.pinyin: meh en-SEH-nyah OH-trah. DEE-gah-meh see loh DEE-goh mahl
steps.pt: Teach me another? Tell me if I say it wrong.
steps.tts: ¿Me enseña otra? Dígame si lo digo mal.

steps.promptPt: Close it in Spanish, which is where you actually live. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you very much, really.

steps.promptPt: Ask for the word before you need it. Speak now.
steps.pt: How do you say thank you?

steps.es: ¿Qué lengua es esa? Solo esa palabra, pero la quería decir bien. ¿Me enseña otra?
steps.pinyin: keh LEN-gwah ehs EH-sah. SOH-loh EH-sah pah-LAH-brah, PEH-roh lah keh-REE-ah deh-SEER byen. meh en-SEH-nyah OH-trah
steps.pt: Shadow asking, being honest about what you know, and asking to learn more.
steps.tts: ¿Qué lengua es esa? Solo esa palabra, pero la quería decir bien. ¿Me enseña otra?

steps.pt: A05 complete. Sixty-eight languages, four accents, one courtesy word in the right place — and honesty about it.

secoes.titulo: The languages are current, not historical
secoes.corpo: Nahuatl and the Maya languages have millions of speakers between them and are used daily, at home and at work. Treating them as relics of the past is the single most common visitor error, and it is audible in how the question gets asked.

secoes.titulo: Match the word to the region
secoes.corpo: Dyos bo'otik belongs in the Yucatán, tlazocamati in Nahuatl-speaking central Mexico. A Maya word said in Oaxaca or a Nahuatl word in Mérida is a small, harmless mistake — but it lands as a costume rather than as courtesy.

secoes.titulo: The four accents you'll actually notice
secoes.corpo: Central Mexico is fast and clipped, with mande as the polite catch-all. Coastal Veracruz lifts and sings. Yucatecan Spanish carries Maya intonation and vocabulary. Northern Spanish has its own rhythm and address words. None is more correct than another.

The reason one word works is that it makes no claim. The moment you let a compliment stand as if you spoke the language, you have taken a warm exchange and put a small lie in the middle of it — so answer the compliment honestly and the moment keeps its value.

permissao: You are allowed to say exactly one word and stop. Nobody expects a visitor to speak Maya or Nahuatl, and a single courtesy word said correctly is worth more here than three sentences of Spanish said fast.
espelho: You already know how it feels when a visitor makes a genuine, slightly clumsy attempt at one word of your own language — it doesn't read as showing off, it reads as effort, and it changes the temperature of the exchange. That is the whole mechanism here, pointed in the other direction.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Two people beside you switch out of Spanish into a language you don't recognise, and you feel as though something is being kept from you.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They switched so I wouldn't understand — either they're talking about me or they'd rather I weren't here.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: In much of Mexico, bilingualism in Spanish and an Indigenous language is ordinary, and speakers switch according to who they are addressing rather than to exclude. What you witnessed was one person speaking to another person in the language they share, which is what happened before you arrived and will happen after you leave.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask what the language is, with curiosity rather than surprise, and let them tell you as much as they want to.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: A moment you were reading as exclusion becomes the most interesting conversation of your day, and often an offer to teach you a word.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not an invitation to ask people to perform their language on demand or to keep pressing once someone gives a short answer — plenty of speakers have had that language treated as a curiosity their whole lives.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You use your one Maya word, someone says 'you speak Maya!', and it feels rude to correct them.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Letting the compliment stand is the gracious move; contradicting it would be false modesty.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The compliment is genuine warmth at the effort, not a factual assessment — and letting it stand converts a small true gesture into a claim you can't back up, which is exactly what makes the next thirty seconds awkward when a second Maya sentence arrives.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say plainly that it's one word and that you wanted to say it properly. That keeps both the effort and the honesty.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The exchange stays warm and usually turns into them teaching you a second word, which is a much better outcome than the polite retreat.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a reason to disclaim every compliment about your Spanish — with Spanish you are genuinely learning the language, and accepting encouragement there is simply accurate.
